audience: HTTP/API engineers learning to reason about API gateways in an interview-sized architecture.
prerequisites: An HTTP client sends a request with a method, path, headers and optional body to a server and receives a response with a status and optional body. HTTPS encrypts HTTP in transit.
An API server can read or write a database. A transaction commits related writes together or aborts them; a committed write can remain stored even if the caller does not receive a response.

objectives.description: Define an API gateway as a client-facing intermediary that forwards API requests and applies shared entry policies; define a backend service as the application handling a request and replicas as copies serving the same role. Trace the request and response. Distinguish choosing an API service and applying policies from load balancing traffic across replicas, while allowing one product to perform both roles.

Define routing as selecting a destination from request properties and an edge policy as a rule applied at the system entrance. Explain method/path routing, the need to read decrypted HTTP for HTTP-aware rules, and rejection before forwarding. Use request-size limits as a concrete policy, explain why shared policies reduce duplication, and retain application-specific validation and business decisions in the service.

Define authentication as checking who a caller is and authorization as deciding what that caller may do. Explain validating credentials at the gateway, conveying trusted identity to a backend, rejecting client-supplied identity claims, and preventing direct paths that bypass required gateway checks. Require the service owning a resource to enforce access to that particular resource; authentication alone does not grant that access.

Define throttling as limiting request rate, a quota as an allowance over a stated period, a burst as a short surge, and scope as the callers and gateway instances sharing a limit. Explain per-user limits, rate rejection and retry delay, why independent local counters can multiply a nominal allowance across replicas, and why best-effort throttling is not strict quota accounting. A strict shared quota needs coordinated accounting with availability and latency costs; request-count limits do not guarantee backend capacity.

Define a timeout as how long a caller waits, an overall deadline as the latest useful response time, and in-flight work as requests already underway. Fit gateway-to-service waits inside the caller's overall budget while leaving time to return a response. Explain that a timeout or gateway error does not establish whether a backend write committed or cancel work already underway.

Define retry amplification as several layers multiplying attempts, an idempotency key as one stable identifier for a logical operation, and deduplication as recognizing repeats. Assign one retry owner with bounded attempts and delayed retries inside the deadline. Require the service owning a write effect to coordinate that effect atomically with a durable duplicate/result record shared across its replicas; a gateway cannot infer safe write retries merely from a timeout or a key.

Define aggregation as combining several backend responses into one client response and fan-out as the resulting multiple calls. Explain a combined response containing required data from one service and optional data from another, its reduction in client calls, its additional dependency/capacity cost, and an explicit deadline and partial-response policy. Missing optional data must be identified, while missing required data fails the response; never silently present incomplete results as complete.

Explain the gateway as an added network hop, operating/configuration responsibility and possible common failure point. Define headroom as spare capacity. Require reachable alternate gateway instances and enough surviving gateway/backend capacity, while acknowledging shared dependencies and bad shared policies. Explain why a gateway is neither complete application security nor new backend capacity, and when one adequate API can apply its own policies without a separate gateway.

questions.question: The Notes app has a Notes service with two replicas and an Authors service. A client-facing gateway sends /notes to Notes and /authors to Authors and rejects oversized request bodies. Trace a successful request and response through the gateway; distinguish this service routing and shared policy role from choosing a Notes replica, including whether one product could do both. State what visibility method/path and body-size rules require for HTTPS, when an oversized request should be rejected, and why note-specific business validation still belongs in the service.
criteria: Traces client to gateway to the selected backend and response through the gateway to the client.
Distinguishes selecting the service and applying shared entry policies from balancing traffic across replicas, while allowing a product to implement both.
HTTP-aware rules require access to decrypted HTTP; rejects an oversized request before forwarding it to the application.
Shared entry rules reduce repeated checks across services but do not replace validation of note-specific business rules by the Notes service.
criticalMisconceptions: An API gateway and a load balancer have mutually exclusive capabilities.
Routing and body inspection can always operate on encrypted HTTP without decryption.
A gateway removes the need for application validation.

questions.question: Alice signs in and asks to read Bob's private note. Her client also sends a header claiming to be Bob, and the Notes service has a direct address that clients can reach. Explain authentication versus authorization, what the gateway must validate and do with the client-supplied identity header, how the service can trust forwarded identity, and how to close or protect the direct path. Identify who must check permission for this particular note and explain why successful gateway authentication is insufficient.
criteria: Authentication establishes the caller's identity through validated credentials; authorization determines whether that identity may access this specific note.
Does not trust the client-supplied identity header; the gateway removes or replaces untrusted identity claims using the validated identity.
The backend accepts forwarded identity only over a trusted, protected gateway-to-service path that prevents callers from impersonating the gateway.
Blocks direct external backend access or subjects that path to equivalent identity and policy checks; a public bypass cannot skip required checks.
The Notes service checks Alice's access to Bob's note and denies it absent permission; a valid identity alone grants no per-note access.
criticalMisconceptions: A signed-in user may read any note.
An identity header is trustworthy merely because it is named by the gateway convention.
Gateway checks protect a backend even when an unchecked direct path remains available.

questions.question: The Notes app promises at most 100 accepted requests per user per minute, but each of two gateway replicas independently allows 100. Explain the intended limit's scope and how routing the same user to both replicas can exceed it. Compare best-effort rate throttling, short bursts and a strict per-period quota; describe the coordination and one cost needed for strict shared accounting. Explain how a client should react to a rate-limit rejection, and why even a correctly enforced request-count limit cannot guarantee that an expensive Notes query fits backend capacity.
criteria: The promised scope is one user's combined traffic across replicas in the stated period; independent counters may admit 200, so their nominal 100 is not a shared strict bound.
Distinguishes rate control and possible short bursts from an exact allowance over a stated period; best-effort throttling is not proof of strict quota enforcement.
Strict shared admission requires coordinated accounting that cannot independently spend the same allowance, adding coordination latency or an availability dependency.
Respects rejection and any supplied retry delay rather than immediately retrying; any retry remains bounded.
Request counts omit unequal request cost and downstream bottlenecks, so limits help protect capacity without guaranteeing sufficient capacity.
criticalMisconceptions: Independent per-replica counters automatically enforce one global allowance.
A best-effort throttle guarantees an exact billing or business quota.
A request-count limit proves the backend cannot overload.

questions.question: A client has a two-second overall budget for creating a note. The gateway forwards the write; the service commits it but its response is lost. Explain how the gateway's service wait should fit inside that budget, what a timeout tells the client, and whether it cancels the write. If both the client and gateway can each make three total attempts, explain the possible attempt amplification and choose one retry owner with bounded attempts and delay inside the budget. Describe the stable operation key and durable shared duplicate/result record atomically coordinated with the note creation by the owning service, and explain why a gateway-only key or a new key on every attempt is insufficient.
criteria: The downstream wait must leave time within the caller's overall deadline for gateway work and returning a response; retries consume the same remaining budget.
A timeout means no response arrived in time, not that the write failed or was canceled; the caller has an unknown outcome even though this scenario's write committed.
Three client attempts each triggering three gateway attempts can produce nine backend attempts; assigns one owner and bounds/delays its attempts to avoid multiplying load.
Reuses one idempotency key for the same logical creation and has the owning service recognize the recorded result across replicas without repeating the effect.

The durable duplicate/result record and effect must be coordinated atomically to handle crashes and concurrent repeats; a gateway-only key lacks effect coordination and a new key does not identify a repeat.
criticalMisconceptions: A gateway timeout proves the note was not saved.
Timing out automatically cancels backend work.
Retries at multiple layers cost no additional backend work.
An idempotency header alone guarantees safe note creation.

questions.question: To show a Notes overview, the gateway calls Notes for required note data and Authors for optional display names, then combines the results. Explain aggregation and fan-out, the client benefit and added backend/dependency cost. Authors stalls: choose an explicit deadline and partial-response policy, explain how the response should represent missing display names, and explain how the policy changes if Notes rather than Authors fails.
criteria: Combines multiple backend results into one client response, reducing client calls while creating multiple backend calls and additional dependencies.
Bounds dependency waits within the overall response budget rather than letting one slow optional call hold the response indefinitely.
Can return required notes with a clear fallback or explicit indication that optional names are unavailable, rather than silently claiming complete data.
Fails the overview when required Notes data is unavailable under the declared contract; does not invent notes or disguise required-data loss as a complete successful response.
criticalMisconceptions: One client request means only one backend operation.
Aggregation removes dependency failures.
Any incomplete response can be labeled complete success without a declared policy.

questions.question: A small Notes app has one adequate API service that already checks identity, permissions and request limits. Explain when a separate gateway may be unnecessary and what changed needs could justify it. The app later uses one gateway in front of several services: explain the extra latency/operating cost, what must remain reachable and have enough spare capacity after a gateway fails, and why adding gateway replicas cannot by itself fix a saturated Notes database, a bad shared routing rule, or missing per-note authorization.
criteria: One adequate API with suitable local policies may not need a separate gateway; multiple services or a useful shared routing/policy boundary can justify it.
Identifies an additional hop and operating/configuration responsibility as costs rather than assuming the component is free.
Requires a reachable alternate gateway path and enough surviving gateway and backend capacity; merely counting replicas does not establish availability.
Gateway replicas do not create database capacity, correct a shared bad policy or enforce omitted per-note permission logic; shared failures and service responsibilities remain.
criticalMisconceptions: Every API architecture requires a separate API gateway.
Gateway replicas guarantee availability regardless of entry routing, capacity or shared failures.
A gateway provides complete application security or creates backend capacity.

cards.objective: Trace an API request and response through a gateway and distinguish shared API entry responsibilities from traffic distribution across replicas.

questions.question: A Notes app has a gateway, a Notes service and two Notes replicas. Trace the request and response, define the gateway, backend service and replicas, distinguish shared API entry policies from replica selection, and state whether one product can perform both gateway and balancing roles.
criteria: Defines the gateway as the intermediary applying shared entry policies and forwarding requests, the backend service as the application handling them, and replicas as copies serving the same role.
Traces client, gateway, backend and response through the gateway.
Distinguishes API entry/policy responsibilities from distributing requests across replicas without declaring the product roles mutually exclusive.
criticalMisconceptions: A gateway must perform the Notes database operation itself.

cards.objective: Route HTTP requests to the right service and apply shared entry rules before forwarding, retaining application-specific decisions in the service.

questions.question: A gateway routes /notes and /authors to different services and imposes a body-size limit. Define routing and edge policy, explain the HTTP visibility required for these HTTPS rules and when to reject an oversized body, then explain the benefit of central rules and why Notes-specific business validation still belongs in Notes.
criteria: Routing selects a destination from request properties; an edge policy is a rule at the system entrance.
The gateway needs access to decrypted HTTP and rejects oversized bodies before application forwarding.
Shared rules reduce duplication across services but cannot replace note-specific business validation.
criticalMisconceptions: A gateway can inspect encrypted HTTP contents without obtaining decrypted contents.

cards.objective: Separate identity verification from per-resource permissions and protect the trusted identity path against forged claims and gateway bypass.

questions.question: Alice requests Bob's private note and supplies a header claiming to be Bob. Define authentication and authorization; explain credential checking, handling the forged header, how Notes trusts forwarded identity and protects any direct access path, and who checks Alice's permission for Bob's note.
criteria: Defines authentication as validating who the caller is and authorization as deciding permitted actions or resource access.
Checks credentials and removes or replaces untrusted identity claims with validated identity; Notes trusts it only through a protected gateway-to-service path.
Blocks direct bypass or enforces equivalent checks there; Notes checks the particular note permission and denies unauthorized access.
criticalMisconceptions: Successful authentication authorizes every note.
Any caller-provided identity header can be trusted.

cards.objective: Reason about per-user throttling, bursts and strict quota accounting across gateway replicas without mistaking request counts for capacity guarantees.

questions.question: Two gateway replicas each allow one user 100 requests per minute independently. Define throttling, quota, burst and limit scope; explain why this does not enforce a shared strict 100 allowance, how strict shared accounting changes coordination and its cost, how to react to rate rejection, and why costly requests can still overload Notes.
criteria: Defines rate control, an allowance over a stated period, a short surge, and the callers/instances sharing the limit.
Independent counters can admit 200; best-effort rate controls differ from exact shared quotas, which require coordinated accounting and incur latency or availability cost.
Respects a rejection and retry delay with bounded retries rather than immediate repeats.
Request counts do not measure unequal work or eliminate downstream bottlenecks.
criticalMisconceptions: Local throttles automatically enforce a strict global quota.

cards.objective: Budget downstream waits within the caller's deadline and distinguish a timeout from cancellation or a known write outcome.

questions.question: A client will wait two seconds to create a note. Define timeout, overall deadline and in-flight work; explain how to budget the gateway's backend wait, what the client can conclude if no response arrives, and whether timing out proves the note was not committed or cancels backend work.
criteria: Defines the waiting limit, latest useful response time and work already underway.
Leaves time for gateway processing and response delivery within the overall budget.
A timeout gives an unknown write outcome and does not by itself cancel work or undo a commit.
criticalMisconceptions: Timeout means the write failed and no note exists.

cards.objective: Assign bounded retry ownership and place durable, atomic duplicate prevention with the service owning the write effect.

questions.question: A note creation times out. Client and gateway each allow three total attempts. Define retry amplification and calculate the possible backend attempts, choose one retry owner with limits and delay inside the deadline, then define idempotency key and deduplication and explain the owning service's shared durable record and atomic coordination. Why are a gateway-only key and a fresh key per retry insufficient?
criteria: Nested attempts can multiply to nine; one owner uses bounded delayed retries within the remaining budget.
One stable key identifies one logical operation and deduplication recognizes repeats.
The effect-owning service atomically coordinates creation with a durable duplicate/result record accessible across replicas so repeats return the recorded result.
Gateway-only keys do not coordinate the actual effect; fresh keys do not identify repeated attempts at the same operation.
criticalMisconceptions: A gateway can make an arbitrary write retry-safe by adding a header.

cards.objective: Combine responses from multiple services with a bounded deadline and explicit required-versus-optional failure policy.

questions.question: A gateway combines required note data with optional author display names. Define aggregation and fan-out, explain the client benefit and backend cost, and choose deadline and partial-response behavior when Authors stalls. How must missing names be represented, and what changes when required Notes data fails?
criteria: Aggregation combines responses; fan-out makes several backend calls, saving client calls but adding backend work and dependencies.
Bounds waits within the response deadline and clearly marks optional missing names or supplies an explicit fallback.
Fails when required note data is unavailable instead of presenting missing required data as a complete result.
criticalMisconceptions: Aggregation makes all dependency failures harmless.

cards.objective: Choose a gateway for concrete needs while accounting for its cost, reachable failover path, surviving capacity and shared security/availability limits.

questions.question: Compare one adequate Notes API with an architecture using a gateway and several services. Explain when to omit or add the gateway and its latency/operating costs. Define headroom and explain the reachable alternate path and surviving capacity required after gateway failure; why can gateway replicas not fix a saturated database, bad shared routing policy or missing per-note authorization?
criteria: A single adequate API can enforce its own policies; shared routing/policies across services can justify a gateway, with an extra hop and operating responsibility.
Headroom is spare capacity; failure handling requires a reachable alternate gateway and enough surviving gateway/backend capacity.
Gateway replication neither removes downstream bottlenecks and shared policy failures nor supplies omitted resource permission checks.
criticalMisconceptions: A gateway is mandatory and guarantees availability or complete security.
